Listen to this article Share AI governance can look impressive from the boardroom. There may be a policy, a steering committee, an approved framework and regular presentations from management. Yet none of these proves that the organisation is making better decisions about AI. Governance is working when it reveals what matters, challenges weak assumptions and enables timely intervention. The first warning sign is not that an AI system has failed. It is that the organisation cannot see clearly enough to know whether it is failing. Here are seven signs that deserve board attention. First, no one can present a credible picture of where AI is being used. The list may cover major projects but exclude AI embedded in purchased software, introduced by vendors or adopted directly by employees. This creates a dangerous gap between authorised AI and actual AI. IBM reported in 2025 that one in five surveyed organisations had experienced a breach involving shadow AI, while only 37 per cent had policies for managing or detecting it. A useful board-level view should identify material AI uses, their purposes, owners, affected stakeholders and dependencies, not catalogue every minor tool. Second, management reports adoption without demonstrating value. Numbers of pilots, licences, users and automated processes may indicate activity, but not business value. The board needs to understand what each material investment is expected to improve and whether those improvements are occurring. Faster processing may look positive until error rates, customer complaints or remediation costs are considered. Value should be evaluated alongside organisational readiness and the exposure accepted in pursuing it. Third, accountability becomes difficult to locate. AI frequently crosses business, technology, legal, risk, data and vendor relationships. Collaboration is essential, but collective involvement can obscure individual accountability. When an AI-supported decision causes harm, “the committee approved it” is insufficient. For every material use, it should be clear who is accountable for its purpose, suitability and continued operation, and who has authority to intervene when concerns arise. Fourth, governance reviews rarely change anything. If every proposal is approved, every risk is declared manageable and every exception is accepted, governance may be confirming management’s intentions rather than testing them. If AI governance never changes a decision, it may be validating management’s intentions rather than governing them. Directors should ask for examples of initiatives that were delayed, redesigned, restricted or declined because the evidence did not support the original proposal. Effective governance should leave fingerprints on decisions. Fifth, vendor confidence is mistaken for organisational assurance. A provider may supply testing results, certifications and technical documentation. Those materials are useful, but they are not sufficient on their own to establish whether the system is appropriate for the organisation’s customers, market, data or operating environment. This is particularly important where institutions depend on a small number of cloud, model or platform providers. Management should be able to explain what has been independently established, what remains dependent on the vendor and what options exist if performance, terms or strategic interests change. Sixth, the board receives conclusions without seeing contrary evidence. A green dashboard can conceal important uncertainty. Directors need visibility into system limitations, incidents, overrides, customer complaints, dissenting assessments and assumptions that are becoming less reliable. The question is not simply whether a system is “performing as expected”, but what that statement excludes. Board reporting should distinguish what management knows, what it believes and what remains untested. It should also show whether independent review supports the claims being made. Seventh, nothing is ever paused or retired. AI systems do not remain fixed. Data changes, models are updated, employees develop new patterns of reliance and systems are extended beyond their original purpose. Approval at deployment must not become permanent permission. Management should define in advance the evidence that would justify scaling, require additional safeguards, trigger restriction or retire it. Sunk investment and executive sponsorship should not make an AI use immune to reconsideration. These signs should not become another checklist completed once a year. They are prompts for a more disciplined conversation about whether governance is influencing the organisation’s real decisions. Boards do not need flawless systems or risk-free innovation. They need confidence that management can identify material AI use, connect it to business value, establish accountability, test vendor claims, surface uncomfortable evidence and change direction when continued use is no longer justifiable. A policy shows that governance has been designed. Evidence that the organisation can challenge, intervene and change course shows that governance is working. That is the difference between AI governance that exists and AI governance that makes the enterprise more defensible. Amaka Ibeji is a Boardroom Certified Qualified Technology Expert and a Digital Trust Visionary. She is the founder of PALS Hub, a digital trust and assurance company.
